blocks.text: 04-BRD / brand Goes here. The structural and strategic foundations of brand identity. Covers brand architecture models (monolithic, endorsed, pluralistic), naming conventions (founder, descriptive, fabricated, metaphor, acronym, magic spell), tagline categories (imperative, descriptive, superlative, provocative, specific), and brandmark typologies (wordmarks, letterforms, pictorial, abstract, emblems, dynamic marks, characters). Also includes the "Brand Ideals" framework (vision, meaning, authenticity, coherence, flexibility, commitment, value, differentiation, sustainability) and cross-cultural identity translation. Not here. • Mapping specific customer touchpoints and moments of truth -> 17-CXP • Community management and organic social media policies -> 13-ORG • Package engineering and raw materials sourcing -> 18-COG

Topics. brand architecture / monolithic, endorsed, and pluralistic frameworks; naming / founder, descriptive, fabricated, metaphor, acronym, and magic spell categories; taglines / imperative, descriptive, superlative, provocative, and specific structures; brandmarks / sequence of cognition (shape, color, form), wordmarks, letterforms, pictorial, abstract, emblems, dynamic, and character marks; brand ideals / vision, meaning, authenticity, coherence, flexibility, commitment, value, differentiation, sustainability; cross-cultural / objective, subjective, and cultural variables in global brand adaptation. Look for. Distinct categorizations of brand architecture (e.g., Monolithic = FedEx; Pluralistic = Yum Brands). The sequence of visual cognition (shape -> color -> form) validating visual processing speed. Specific classifications of taglines and names. Explicit definitions of brand ideals. Skip. Vague platitudes about "design is good business." General history of specific logos unless providing a structural framework. Scope mix. 80% baseline (the foundational definitions of brand marks, names, and architecture), 20% growth (dynamic marks, private labeling strategy, brand licensing). Volume. 500 to 700 words.

17-CXP / post-purchase and experience Goes here. Designing the brand experience as a distinct economic offering. Identifying and curating customer touchpoints, mapping "moments of truth," and applying the five principles of experience design (ubiquitous, social, semantic, sentient, human). Not here. • Visual identity design, logo files, and typography standards -> 04-BRD • Developing the responsive grid for web or mobile apps -> 07-LPG

Topics. customer experience / touchpoint mapping, moments of truth, experience as a distinct economic offering; design principles / ubiquitous, social, semantic, sentient, and human. Look for. Definitions of specific touchpoints and the chronological mapping of the "moment of truth" (e.g., sighting the hotel from the highway -> walking into the front lobby -> glimpsing into the room). Skip. General praise for basic customer service or vague assertions about "delighting the customer" without a structural framework. Scope mix. 40% baseline (identifying touchpoints), 60% growth (engineering sentient/semantic brand experiences). Volume. 200 to 300 words.

13-ORG / organic and social Goes here. Organic social media strategy, disclosure checklists, community building, crisis communications planning, reputation management, and personal branding ("Me Inc."). Not here. • Paid social media campaigns and ad creatives -> 10-MCR • Visual brand identity and logo files -> 04-BRD

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Provides a structured crisis communications checklist and specific disclosure best practices for managing brand reputation in organic social environments. modules: [ORG] topics: [social media strategy, disclosure best practices, crisis communications, reputation management, personal branding] tier: 2 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. social media strategy / the 5 steps to a social strategy (objective, community building, content, management, measurement); disclosure / over-disclosure rules, avoiding social media loopholes; crisis communications / proactive planning, establishing a 24/7 microsite, key message alignment, transparent engagement protocols; personal branding / managing "Me Inc." and career reputation. Look for. The specific Crisis Communications checklist (e.g., establishing organizational protocols for determining a crisis, 24/7 social monitoring schedules, "do not delete negative comments"). Social media disclosure best practices. Skip. Broad statements about how "social media has changed the world" or vanity metrics without qualitative assessment frameworks. Scope mix. 70% baseline (crisis prep, disclosure rules), 30% growth (advanced community building). Volume. 300 to 400 words.

Sally Hudson Marketing Consultant 11 Branding imperatives Reasons to invest in brand identity Make it easy for the customer to buy Compelling brand identity presents any company, any size, anywhere with an immediately recognizable, distinctive professional image that positions it for success. An identity helps manage the perception of a company and differentiates it from its competitors. A smart system conveys respect for the customer and makes it easy to understand features and benefits. A new product design or a better environment can delight a customer and create loyalty. An effective identity encompasses such elements as a name that is easy to remember or a distinctive package design for a product. Make it easy for the sales force to sell Whether it is the CEO of a global conglomerate communicating a new vision to the board, a firsttime entrepreneur pitching to venture capital firms, or a financial advisor creating a need for investment products, everyone is selling. Nonprofits, whether fundraising or soliciting new volunteers, are continually selling. Strategic brand identity works across diverse audiences and cultures to build an awareness and understanding of a company and its strengths. By making intelligence visible, effective identity seeks to communicate a company’s unique value proposition. The coherence of communications across various media sends a strong signal to the customer about the laserlike focus of a company. Make it easy to build brand equity The goal of all public companies is to increase shareholder value. A brand, or a company’s reputation, is considered to be one of the most valuable company assets. Small companies and nonprofits also need to build brand equity. Their future success is dependent on building public awareness, preserving their reputations, and upholding their value. A strong brand identity will help build brand equity through increased recognition, awareness, and customer loyalty, which in turn helps make a company more successful. Managers who seize every opportunity to communicate their company’s brand value and what the brand stands for sleep better at night. They are building a precious asset. Acknowledge that we live in a branded world. Seize every opportunity to position your company in your customers’ minds. Communicate a strong brand idea over and over again. Go beyond declaring a competitive advantage. Demonstrate it! Understand the customers. Build on their perceptions, preferences, dreams, values, and lifestyles. Use brand identity to create sensory magnets to attract and retain customers. 12 Brand strategy Effective brand strategy provides a central, unifying idea around which all behavior, actions, and communications are aligned. It works across products and services, and is effective over time. The best brand strategies are so differentiated and powerful that they deflect the competition. They are easy to talk about, whether you are the CEO or an employee. Brand strategy builds on a vision, is aligned with business strategy, emerges from a company’s values and culture, and reflects an in-depth understanding of the customer’s needs and perceptions. Brand strategy defines positioning, differentiation, the competitive advantage, and a unique value proposition. Brand strategy needs to resonate with all stakeholders: external customers, the media, and internal customers (for example, employees, the board, core suppliers). Brand strategy is a road map that guides marketing, makes it easier for the sales force to sell more, and provides clarity, context, and inspiration to employees. See the world through the customer’s eyes. It often takes someone from the outside who is an experienced strategic and creative thinker to help a company articulate what is already there. Sometimes a brand strategy is born at the inception of a company by a visionary, such as Steve Jobs, Jeff Bezos, or Anita Roddick. Sometimes it takes a visionary team to redefine brand strategy.
